The statement acknowledges a large, adverse shock to demand and credit conditions from COVID-19, which the literature shows can be amplified via financial frictions: tighter credit and weaker firm balance sheets raise external finance premia and deepen recessions (credit/financial accelerator view). The Fed’s response—cutting the federal funds rate to the effective lower bound, initiating large-scale purchases of Treasuries and agency MBS, expanding repo operations, lowering the discount rate, easing reserve requirements, and reopening/densifying dollar swap lines—directly targets liquidity constraints and transmission through long-duration assets and credit spreads, consistent with lender-of-last-resort and credit-channel stabilization prescriptions. With market-based inflation compensation falling and survey expectations little changed, aggressive easing is aligned with inflation-targeting and expectations-management principles to guard against deflation risk while maintaining credibility. However, at the zero lower bound the economy is vulnerable to a liquidity trap; effectiveness hinges on expectations and the credit channel, so near-term activity still faces material downside risk even with policy support. Overall sentiment remains negative but is moderated by the policy actions.
